foreword: This project began during the COVID quarantine as a way to fill the day with something other than becoming the ultimate couch potato. We had a lot of hanukkiot on display shelves, but no catalogue of how many of them there were or where they’d come from. Ana thought Jim should take a picture of each one and set up some sort of database that might be useful to our children. So Jim took out his camera and a tripod and started posing the them to take their portraits. They were mostly cooperative.
introduction:
A “menorah” is simply a candleholder. These are “hanukkiot” - menorahs designed for the celebration Hanukkah. While they are may take very different forms, each has places for 9 lights. Eight of the lights represent the nights of the festival and one, the “shamash”, is the caretaker used to light the others. The earliest hanukkiot were designed to use oil with simple wicks. Today most are lit by candles, but a few are now using LEDs.

We’ve adopted the most widely accepted transliterations for the name of the holiday (Hanukkah) and the candelabra (hanukiah in the singular and hanukkiot in plural).

Each is a unique work of art. Because we don’t always know the name given to them by their creators, we’ve made up names that we like to think fit them.

Collections are strange things, sometimes they develop their own minds. You acquire a single thing that tickles your funny bone; tells a good story; reminds you of something special; enchants you with its look, feel or history; or speaks to your hopes and fears. Then somehow you find you’ve acquired another, and another, and another. Suddenly you’ve got a collection. Our collection has been accumulating that way for a long time now - and we’re pleased to share it. We hope you get as much pleasure from them as we do.

sections.title: Many Shapes, Sizes and Stories
sections.intro: Hanukkiot tell stories. The primary story each tells is of the Maccabees and the reconsecration of the Temple. Their creators frequently extend that basic story and create art with it. Sometimes the story is obvious, other times it requires the observer to look closely. Colors, shapes and even the material used become carriers of additional meanings.

items.title: The Saint Louis
items.caption: In May 1939, the SS St. Louis left Germany with more than 900 Jews aboard, headed for Cuba, fleeing Nazi persecution. After waiting 5 days in Havana harbor, only 28 passengers were allowed to disembark. The rest were turned away. The ship attempted to dock in Miami but was denied entry. The captain refused to return to Germany and eventually docked in Antwerp. Passengers were dispersed to the UK, France, the Netherlands, and the ship returned to Hamburg empty. It’s estimated that approximately one-third of the passengers were victims of the Holocaust. We see this terracotta sculpture as representative of their despair.

items.title: The Factory
items.caption: We find this piece both profoundly moving and profoundly disturbing. Crafted by “The Clockworks,” it may be a benign representation of a factory with smokestacks and people engaged in various activities. Or it may be a metaphorical representation of Auschwitz, with the crematory towers and figures representing Holocaust victims. The triangle was one of the badges victims of the Nazis were required to wear.

items.title: Synagogues of Europe
items.caption: The synagogue was the center of Jewish life in many cities. Here are nine different famous European synagogues placed side by side. From the left they are Prague, Toledo, Dubrovnik, Cracow, Vilna, Lutsk, Zabludow, Budapest and Florence. We’ve visited four over the years. We looked up Zabludow and discovered we knew the city as Bialystock.

items.title: Serenity
items.caption: We think it looks a little like the artist dropped a stone in a quiet pond and watched as the ripples spread from the center outwards.  Just sitting and quietly watching as the candles burn down can restore harmony after a tumultuous day - and that is a gift in and of itself.

items.title: Circle Game
items.caption: This was a special gift from ourselves to ourselves the first year we were married. Circles are a symbol of completeness, and joining two of them, slightly offset, with the base for the candles is a brilliant design. The heavy glass is tinted red and black and demands fancy candles.

items.title: The Wailing Wall
items.caption: The Wailing Wall came from the gift shop at Temple Israel of New Rochelle long before we were together. Allegedly comprised of Jerusalem stone and hand-formed pottery jugs, it was purchased at the Judaica shop at Temple Israel of New Rochelle, sometime in the mid-1980s. Theoretically, one can use oil to fill the jugs, pop in a wick, and light it up. We prefer to use candles.

items.title: The Magic School Bus
items.caption:
What makes this school bus magic is where it comes from. It was presented to us by the students in Room 1 at the JCC of Mid-Westchester.

We are so lucky to have you as our friends. Thank you for this wonderful addition to our collection. There are other hanukkiot from the JCCMW included in the final section.

items.title: Silver Reflections
items.caption: Formed of flat silver plates bolted and then soldered together this piece throws the candles’ lights in glorious reflections. It is also a pain in the butt to keep polished. It probably came from Colonial Williamsburg around the turn of the millennium.

items.title: Octahedronorah
items.caption: We went to the Jewish Museum in New York City to see the exhibit on Leonard Cohen. The show was wonderful - informative and engaging. Just like the Jewish Museum in Paris, one exits through the Gift Shop. As we did, we saw the Octahedron and knew we had to make it a part of our collection. Each of the eight sides has the correct number of candleholders - a blessing for anyone who forgets what day it is.

items.title: Tangramenorah
items.caption: Unbeknownst to one another, Denise and Jonina each chose the Tangramenorah from the Museum of Modern Art store as the perfect Hanukkah gift for us in 2020. The nine pieces of pre-cast concrete can be stored in a triangular oblong that has the shape of a Toblerone bar, if one can figure it out. Arranging them for use is much easier. We got two. Did we actually need two? Which one did we return? We’ll never tell.

items.title: Tradition! Tradition!
items.caption: Everyone and her grandmother had a variation on this design when we were growing up. It was a “modern” piece, meant to either replace or complement an existing hanukiah. This one was probably Jim’s maternal grandmother’s. It’s brass with a gold finish and can only be used with wax candles. The doors on the Ark open from the center to reveal the 10 Commandments.

items.title: Y’Israel
items.caption: This one actually was Jim’s mother’s, and the first one he remembers. It took him years to figure out it actually said “Y’Israel” as part of its design. (He was never a good Hebrew student.) It’s brass with a greenish enamel overlay, now wearing away in places.

items.title: O Jerusalem
items.caption: Jerusalem’s skyline is the theme for many hanukkiot. This one is cast in heavy brass and is limited to use with candles. The sculpted texture suggests it was created in the middle of the 20th century. Neither of us remembers where this came from, though it probably predates our marriage. We noticed the 3 “Shem” design but have no idea what it may mean.

items.title: The Lions of Judah
items.caption: Like the skyline of Jerusalem, the Lions of Judah often flanking David’s Crown and the Tablets of the Law, is a frequent theme for hanukkiot. We don’t know or can’t remember the origin of some of the items in the collection. In most cases, that’s because they came with Jim when we got married. They are “pre-existing conditions”, and fit subjects for the creation of exotic and/or mysterious origin myths.

items.title: Older Lions of Judah
items.caption: This is another, albeit older, interpretation of the “Lions of Judah” theme. Jim believes it belonged to his paternal grandmother, Tessie. Where and how she originally acquired it is lost in the mists of the past.

sections.title: Craft Fair Finds
sections.intro:
Over the years we’ve bought several beautiful originals from craft fairs.

There are no “brick and mortar” stores we know of that carry only hanukkiot. There are plenty of stores which carry “Judaica” and usually include one or more hanukkiot in their wares - usually either mass-produced commercial pieces or artistic works beyond our budget. Craft fairs however frequently include artists and artisans who make beautiful pieces and offer them at reasonable prices.

items.title: Sew Happiness, Reap Joy
items.caption: This hanukiah is fashioned of cut metal, enameled, and lighted with LED tea lights. We purchased it at the first Bet Am Shalom craft fair we attended. It set the tone for the collection, “Light Up the Universe”.

items.title: Dreidel Included
items.caption: Lyndhurst holds a crafts fair every spring. One year we found this hanukiah. Gambling with a dreidel for Hanukkah gelt is a time-honored tradition, so it makes sense to include a dreidel with the hanukiah. This dreidel can be lifted off and actually used for play, making this a nice all-in-one Hanukkah set. It’s formed and hammered brass with colors somehow added.

items.title: For a Few Shekels More
items.caption: As noted, gambling with a dreidel is a beloved Hanukkah pastime; a practice honored by the theme of this hanukiah. The candleholders are glass reproductions of ancient shekels fitted with wires. The base is glass with indents to hold the coins. Nine coins aren’t really a very big pot, but for a few shekels more…

items.title: Leaves on the Tree of Life
items.caption: The Tree of Life is a very popular motif for hanukkiot. This one is brass with fall-colored brass leaves reaching up from the branches. We found it at a Lyndhurst crafts market and decided it needed to be planted in our house.

items.title: Tree of Life
items.caption: This version is glass and on the delicate side. Bet Am Shalom’s annual craft fair has been a fertile hunting ground for interesting works, and we’ve been lucky enough to acquire a number of pieces from there over the years. The original of this one met an unfortunate end, smashing to the floor while being cleaned. Ana found the artist’s online presence and ordered a replacement.

items.title: You Got Some Brass
items.caption: It’s a slab of polished stone with eight brass reflectors attached at the back edge. The reflectors can be raised or lowered individually, raising the amount of light it throws into the room.

items.title: Rainbow Arch
items.caption: The Rainbow Arch was a favorite with our granddaughter Aurora and grandson Lucian. The candle holders are magnets which can be removed and stuck on other steel surfaces, providing endless hours of amusement. The arched base is polished steel, but obviously not as interesting to children as other surfaces.

items.title: Glass Wall
items.caption: A thick sheet of glass sitting in a cleverly designed holder and topped with copper candleholders. The motif is the ever popular Wailing Wall. The artist signed it “Sylvia S.” Sadly we don’t know who she is or what else she’s created.

items.title: Cups of Joy
items.caption: This was our 2020 acquisition from the Crafts Fair at Bet Am Shalom. Usually, we go and wander around for a few hours and can sometimes talk to the artists. With the COVID-19 pandemic imposing restrictions on gatherings, the show went virtual. While that meant we couldn’t examine the works individually, weighing them in our hands, turning them to view from every angle, it did mean the artists could make video presentations and explain each item in detail. The artist, Frann Addison, explained that she collects odds and ends and then assembles them into pleasing wholes. This is glass and brass and one of only two in our collection that is oil-only.

items.title: Ombre Wave
items.caption: Reminiscent of a castle wall, the candleholders slide along the polished metal edge. The hanukiah has a nice curved shape, and the lower textured portion gains in color from one end to the other. We met the artist, Laura Cowen, at one of Bet Am Shalom’s fairs.

items.title: Cityscape
items.caption: Because we don’t know what the artist was thinking, We’ve dubbed this one “Cityscape”.  We think it looks like an iconic city skyline - even if we can’t identify which city. It’s aluminum, and the holders swivel, allowing an infinite variety of looks.

sections.title: Our Menagerie
sections.intro: Neither of us wants to be responsible for taking care of a pet at this point in our lives. That doesn’t mean we don’t love animals, it means we don’t want to own a living one. On the other hand, looking at them in a zoo or as part of a hanukiah is delightful.

items.title: Noah’s Ark
items.caption: Hanukkah has always had a special appeal for children, and so it’s only to be expected that some hanukkiot come with themes aimed at the young (and the young at heart). This Noah’s Ark is cut metal with brightly colored enamel animals embarking on their journey.

items.title: Noah’s Other Ark
items.caption: Who actually needs Noah on a fantasy Ark when the animals aboard can act as the crew as well as being the passengers? This piece came from the gift store at Temple Israel of New Rochelle in the early 1980s.

items.title: Mergansermenorah
items.caption: Mergansers are fish-eating birds. The connection between this brightly colored specimen, her/his dinner, and Hanukkah completely escapes us, unless the artist was trying to allude to the story of Jonah. On the other hand, children seem captivated by it. This too came from Bet Am Shalom.

items.title: Pachydermenorah
items.caption: When Jonina gave this to us, we looked at each other and said, “Pachydermenorah!” She has enchanted children and adults alike. She also inspired Jim to take her picture and so became the first portrait Jim shot for this collection. She’s from Jonathan Adler, in case you’re wondering.

items.title: Serpentomenorah
items.caption: When we visit Paris, we frequently visit the Jewish Museum, which is conveniently located in the Marais near L’As du Falafel— perhaps the best falafel and gyro restaurant in the universe. We went to the Museum to see a special exhibit on Dreyfus, which commemorated the 20th anniversary of the French Army’s declaration of his innocence. Like all museums, one exits through the gift shop, where we found the Serpentomenorah. It’s a single piece of brass with candle holes drilled in it.

items.title: Menorahsaurus
items.caption: Denise discovered the Menorahsaurus online through an Etsy vendor and snapped him up as a gift for us. We thought it was a fantastic idea, so we went online and purchased another one for grandson Jack, who was totally into dinosaurs at the time. It’s a simple plastic toy dinosaur with candleholders attached along his spine, mounted on a simple wooden base, and painted silver.

items.title: Got His Goat
items.caption: From the akedah to the annual soundings of the shofar, rams seem to have a special place in Jewish tradition, so a hanukiah celebrating one seems a good idea. We found this one at the Jewish Museum of NY online during the second winter of COVID-enforced isolation. His cheerful colors and willingness to provide a perch for the bird cheered us up.

sections.title: Gifts
sections.intro: What do you give someone who has everything they need? For about a decade now daughters Jonina and Denise and their families have answered that question by finding amazing hanukkiot to add to our collection. Each is a treasure. Some are natural fits with other groupings, and are shown there. Others defy easy categorization and are displayed here.

items.title: Bottled Up Holiday Spirit
items.caption: What’s a holiday without a bit of liquid cheer? Daughter Denise gave us this really clever copper design. The copper frame holding the candle cups is set into a cork. To create a unique work of art, one picks an attractive bottle and corks it with the frame. We tried it in a bottle of good Bordeaux but ultimately preferred Denise’s choice of bottle.

items.title: Silver Branches
items.caption: Silver Branches is one of many hanukkiot we’ve received as a gift from our daughter Jonina. Year after year,  we’ve been the beneficiaries of her eye for unusual and beautiful pieces. This one is polished metal and recalls the traditional 4-1-4 configuration. We thought the branches might be stylized Hebrew letters, but we can’t figure out what it might say.

items.title: X Marks the Spot
items.caption: It’s comprised of ten separate pieces, which can be arranged however one wishes. Tic-tac-toe is an interesting metaphor for the game of life. Planning ahead and thinking through the consequences of one’s actions ensures that while one may never win, one never loses either. Our 5783 gift from Jonina and family.

items.title: Folk Us
items.caption: Are these figures a family? They're one short of a minyan. So who are they? Folks just like us, or so it would seem. They are ceramic and each face is slightly different from any of the others. They are freestanding, perhaps allowing each of them to pursue her/his own destiny. Again, a gift from Jonina.

items.title: Silver Bean
items.caption: The Silver Bean is another hanukiah from Jonina. It's actually shaped like half a regular doughnut, not even a Hanukkah-appropriate jelly doughnut. It has a really pleasing shape and substantial heft, and while it retains the 4-1-4 configuration, it’s far from traditional.

items.title: Let’s Be Completely Transparent About This
items.caption: This is another of Jonina’s special finds. It’s glass and the pieces can actually be pushed together, but we think it looks better with a bit of space between each of the elements. It could also be re-arranged from a 4-1-4 configuration to an 8-1.

items.title: Perfectly Clear
items.caption: As opposed to the mobility of the preceding piece, the glass blocks which comprise this one are fixed in place. It’s crystal clarity leaves only two questions - first, should the shamus be on the right or the left? Second, where does Jonina keep finding these wonderful designs?

items.title: Inclined to Celebrate
items.caption: This hanukiah is so simple and so elegant. Polished hardwood and polished steel set at a slight incline. At first glance, we couldn’t figure out which was the shamus - then realized that the candle to the left was set a little farther from its fellows. Technically, this menorah isn’t “kosher” because the shamus is supposed to be raised above the level of the others. We decided that the Creator probably doesn’t care, so we shouldn’t either. Another gift from Jonina.

items.title: Scott Free
items.caption:
This piece was a gift from Rabbi Scott Weiner of Tamid of Westchester.

We’re not sure whether it was designed as a traveling hanukiah, but it is certainly reminiscent of the genre. Like Tamid itself, it is elegantly simple in its conception. Free of any unnecessary distractions one can focus on the meaning.

sections.title: Travel
sections.intro: Over the course of our life together we’ve been privileged to visit more than 60 countries. At some point we decided to make a serious effort to include Jewish cultural and/or historical sites in our travels. Rather than bring home typical tourist tchotckes that would collect dust and fade from consciousness, we decided to try to bring home a hanukiah from each as our souvenir. We haven’t always succeeded, but it hasn’t been for a lack of trying.

items.title: Argentine Beef
items.caption: We went with the American Association of Cantors on a Jewish cultural tour of Argentina. Buenos Aires has a thriving Jewish community. We celebrated a Shabbat at the Libertadt Synagogue, which was founded in 1842. We also visited memorials at the sites of the bombings in 1994 and 1996. Our only beef was that surprisingly there really wasn’t much indigenous Judaica in the market in Buenos Aires.

items.title: S’Fad Rainbow
items.caption: We went to Israel on an ARZA-sponsored trip in 2011 after we were b’nai mitzvot. One of the most interesting places we visited was the artists’ city of S’Fad. Walking down an alleyway, we found a shop which claimed their hanukkiot were made out of discarded war materials - a figurative beating of swords into plowshares. Eschewing ones derived from cartridge casings, we found this one. The creator claimed it was made from Lexan, which is used in the canopies of fighter aircraft, to which he then added colored gels. When he saw our interest and heard why we were visiting, he offered to personalize it for Ana, inscribing her Hebrew name “Chana Ruth” on the base. Then he signed and dated it. We have no idea whether his story was true, but he was a great salesman.

items.title: Some Assembly Required
items.caption: While we were in S’Fad, we saw this unusual Hanukiah. The nine pieces are machined aluminum and store as a single amphora-shaped piece - unless you want to stack them in some other order. They fit together perfectly, providing endless hours of distraction and imaginative play. As a portable Hanukiah, it is a direct descendant of the 15th-century Spanish “Traveling Lights”.

items.title: Murano Glass
items.caption: What goes around comes around. We bought this menorah for Jim’s mother when we visited the ghetto in Florence. Mom loved Murano glass, and we thought it would be a beautiful addition to her collection. After Mom died in February 2010, Dad returned it to us.

items.title: Mounds
items.caption: This one is from the gift shop at the “White Synagogue” in Toledo, Spain. It’s squarish-shaped mounds of clay, painted with silver and gold paint, and sitting on a hardwood platform.

items.title: Strike Up the Band
items.caption: After the October 7, 2023 massacre, we went on a mission to Israel in February 2024. Israeli life during that period was scary, with many people called up for active military duty, leaving streets and shops deserted. It was also remarkably hopeful. In the Mamilla Mall, where we found this piece, we were constantly stopped and thanked for coming - and everyone was looking forward to the rhythms of life resuming their normal beat.

items.title: In Training
items.caption: After two years of delays caused by COVID, we were finally able to take some of the grandchildren on a trip in the summer of 2022. We went by train from London to Paris, and around the corner from the best falafel in Paris (L’As du Falafel, should you ever go), we found the perfect souvenir.

items.title: On the Road to Marrakech
items.caption:
This is one of the two oldest pieces in our collection. It is hammered brass and uses oil and free-floating wicks.

The Jewish community in Morocco mostly left at the end of the last century. We bought this at the Laazama Synagogue, which was founded in 1492. It was selling its artifacts in hopes of raising enough money to refurbish the building so that it can continue to serve its shrinking community.

items.title: Fes Up
items.caption: In March 2026 we returned to Morocco on a Jewish tour with our congregation. We revisited the Laazama Synagogue and were overjoyed to find it beautifully restored. As part of the tour we visited a pottery/ceramics factory in Fez and couldn’t resist this one.

items.title: Traveling Light(s)
items.caption: In Toledo, Spain, near the “White Synagogue”, there was a modest shop filled with antiques and tourist souvenirs. Amidst the “Crusader” swords, “Conquistador" flintlocks, and “pirate” blunderbusses were some genuine items. This is a traveler’s hanukiah from around the time of the Expulsion. It’s silver, about 4” in diameter, and 2” high when the lid is closed.

items.title: London Guildhall
items.caption: We found this unusual piece at a craft show at the London Goldsmith’s Guildhall. The machined metal base embraces a metal plate with a collage of old newspaper clippings. The candle holders are magnets and can be stored in the hollow bottom.

items.title: Simple Russian Village
items.caption: This hanukiah comes from the gift shop in the synagogue in St. Petersburg, Russia. It is a simple painted ceramic with the Jerusalem skyline motif. The artist is Alexander Zvezdin, an Israeli-trained artist who is a native of St. Petersburg.

items.title: Venetian Floating Lights
items.caption: The original ghetto was in Florence, Italy, and described the district in which there was a cannon foundry. The Jews were confined to that area in the early 16th century, and the word ghetto came to mean a place where people were constrained to live by virtue of religion, economic status, or color. The tradition of metalworking and Florence’s canals come together in this hanukiah. There is a little store on one of the corners across from the synagogue with several interesting hanukkiot and other Judaica. The proprietor was charming, and he swore this piece was unique. We bought it only to discover it displayed in numerous other shops throughout the city.

items.title: Children’s Choir
items.caption: The Children’s Choir came from the same shop in the Ghetto where we bought the gondola. We asked if he would ship it home for us, and he absolutely refused. We ended up carrying it, ever so carefully wrapped, for the rest of our trip. It’s hand-painted ceramic and just fun to look at. Unlike the gondola, it was unique to the shop - we never saw another like it anywhere. The artist who created it is Dino Bencini.

items.title: Williamsburg Colonial Style
items.caption: On a visit to Colonial Williamsburg, we saw individual candlesticks in this style. A few months later, we were in Pottery Barn and found this. It’s base metal, and the linkages at the bottom can be folded to create different looks - and they brace candleholders that are really too tall to be stable on their own.

sections.title: Special Circumstances
sections.intro: The MacInnis House hanukiah, the two St. Petersburg hanukkiot as well as the antique pair from the Libertadt Synagogue in Buenos Aires, the Lego® Menorah at the JCC of Mid-Westchester, and the three photographed during our 2024 mission to Israel are the pieces in this collection that we don’t own. Still, they are so beautiful, deeply poignant, and/or historic that they had to be included.

items.title: MacInnis House
items.caption: MacInnis House in Ballard, Washington is home to grandchildren Hannah and Judah. When we visited in October 2025 Jim was sitting with his MacBook at their dining room table editing a draft of this work. Hannah watched, fascinated, over his shoulder. She then went to the bookshelf and brought this one to him and asked whether he wanted to include it. There was only one possible answer - and Hannah designed the candles.

items.title: St. Petersburg
items.caption: In St. Petersburg, Russia, there is a “Museum of Ethnography” in which there are displays of artifacts from each of the many ethnic groups which lived in Russia. Among them are “The Hebrews” - the Russian word for “Jew” being commonly thought of as a vulgarity. The display occupies several large rooms and contains a number of pieces of Judaica, including two hanukkiot. They were displayed in large locked cases at the farthest point from the walkway through the section. Photographing them required a steady hand, a 400mm lens, and much post-processing. I believe this one is in a base metal and is adorned with eagles, though not the two-headed one associated with the Romanovs.

items.title: St. Petersburg Too
items.caption: This is the second piece from the Museum of Ethnography. It’s apparently silver, extremely ornate and contains not only the Crown of David at its top but also winged lions of Judah in the back panel. How the Museum came into possession of the two hanukkiot isn’t clear and leaves us wondering about what happened to the families who owned them.

items.title: Libertadt Italian Bronze
items.caption: Many Jewish families in Argentina emigrated from Italy in the early 19th century and by 1842 founded Libertadt Synagogue in Buenos Aires. This hanukiah is one of two old pieces on display in their museum. We don’t know the significance of the birds, or even what kind they are - but they have found a good place to roost. This piece is attributed as Italian from the late 18th or early 19th century. The Libertadt sanctuary is beautiful - and both exotic and familiar looking, reminding us perhaps that wherever we go we can make a home.

items.title: Libertadt Antique
items.caption: This looks to be a much older creation, so we assume it was an heirloom brought to Argentina by an immigrating family. It appears to be cast bronze and in a style similar to our Moroccan hanukiah. It is clearly meant to use oil, not candles. The faded note explaining it was in completely illegible Spanish, so there isn’t much we can tell about it.

items.title: Iron Swords
items.caption: In 2023 Hanukkah began exactly two months after the October 7th attack. The IDF’s ranks were filled with thousands of reservists, away from their homes and families for the holidays and so without their traditional hanukkiot. Many groups created impromptu hanukkiot out of whatever was at hand to celebrate the holiday. The small placard apparently expresses gratitude to a local military unit and its medical corps for their service following October 7th.

items.title: Moshav Plowshare
items.caption: We visited a moshav which proudly displayed this hanukiah commemorating Hanukkah 2023. It looks to be made of discarded farm tools and perhaps an old plowshare. The arched inscription is biblical and concludes “Let there be light.” We noticed that all of the Israeli hanukkiot we saw on public display carried the secular date of 2023 rather than the Jewish year 5784.

items.title: Hostage Square
items.caption: This piece sits in Hostage Square in Tel Aviv - near the Seder table with empty chairs commemorating the hostages missing from that celebration. Every holiday without them reminds us that to appreciate joy one must also recognize the pain.

sections.title: The JCCMW
sections.intro:
We have a long and wonderful history of involvement with the Jewish Community Center of Mid-Westchester. Jim served on its Board and was President of the Nursery School for many years. A few years ago someone found out about our collection and persuaded him to print several of the pieces in poster size so that they could hang as seasonal decorations in the entry hall during Hanukkah. Seeing the posters, the kids were fascinated by the variety of hanukkiot and asked their teachers questions about them. That led to a request to do a slideshow for the kids with pictures of all of our hanukkiot. The slideshow has become sort of an annual event - and a highlight of our Hanukkah celebration.

The hanukkiot on the next few pages are the work of students at the JCCMW Nursery School. Beginning with the first time Jim shared a slideshow of our collection with the students they responded by sharing their creations of beautiful, handcrafted hanukkiot with us. We are proud to include them in our collection and to share them with you. We’re pretty sure none of the hanukkiot created by the students in the Nursery School  were ever used with lighted candles. When Jim took portraits of them to share with the students he took the liberty of adding lighted candles using the magic of post-processing.

items.title: LEGO® My Hanukiah
items.caption: This hanukiah was assembled, LEGO® brick by LEGO® brick, by volunteers in the Friedland Makerspace at the JCCMW. It stands nearly 5 feet tall; the candleholders look like small cupolas, sort of like shopfronts in the Old City of Jerusalem. It’s wisely lit with LEDs instead of candles.

items.title: Stacks (Room 1 - 5781)
items.caption: It’s made of small plastic building blocks stacked one upon another and then carefully glued in place on a piece of cardboard painted to look like wood. The candleholders are the same as for a birthday cake. Jim asked if he could take it home to make a photograph of it. It was returned to the class with a poster-sized print of the photo.

items.title: Simply Nuts about Hanukkah (Room 1 - 5782)
items.caption: The second year Jim did the slide show the young artists proudly showed their work and asked if Jim would take a picture of it too. He agreed to take it home, photograph it and return it with a large print to hand in the classroom. Someone had figured out that standard nuts were the perfect size to hold the candles. We stayed for the classroom Hanukkah celebration and their stories of how they celebrate at home. They really are simply nuts about the holiday.

items.title: Glass Tiles (Room 1 - 5783)
items.caption: To create their own hanukiah the young artists used materials that were readily available and easy to work with. A small piece of wall tile becomes a marble platform on which they glued decorative glass tiles and bolts to hold the candles. Jim was told he could keep this one for the collection. We just hope that someone’s bathroom renovation project wasn’t short of materials.

items.title: Nuts & Tiles Blue (Room 1 - 5784)
items.caption: In 5784 the slide presentation was extended to two classrooms as the nursery school grew. Each class got its own show with “Mr. Jim” and each classroom presented its own hanukiah as a “thank you.” At first, they look identical, but for the color. Now look again — the line of candles is straight in one, and staggered in the other. (This piece is paired with No. 071, made by the sister classroom the same year.)

items.title: Crayons (JCCMW - 5785)
items.caption: The following year the slide show was extended to the entire nursery school in one assembly. We received this hanukiah from all the students. One of the original reasons for sharing our hanukkiot with the children was to encourage them to see the artistry in ritual objects. We think they get the idea. Decorating their hanukiah with crayons we see as an invitation to create more art.

items.title: All Wrapped Up (JCCMW - 5786)
items.caption: This one is either a holiday card with a stamp, or perhaps a cleverly wrapped Hanukkah present. It came from the artists in the nursery school. It represents the wrapping up of Jim’s board service at the “J”, the secular year and this presentation as well. Chag Sameach!*
